I’ll build a progressive 12-week postpartum return-to-exercise program for a 33‑year‑old female who is 4 weeks post uncomplicated C‑section and has been cleared only for light activity (walking, no abdominal work, no heavy lifting, no jumping) until the routine 6‑week OB check. Program assumes home environment, mat only. This plan is conservative, progressive, and designed to prioritize pelvic floor and transversus abdominis recovery, scar tissue mobilization (gentle), posture, breathing, mobility, and low‑impact strength that respects the 6‑week restriction. Include guidance for returning to more intense exercise after clearance.

Important notes / contraindications (read before using):
- Continue to follow medical advice from her OB. If she experiences pain (especially pelvic pain), heavy bleeding, dizziness, faintness, fever, worsening incision pain, new urinary/fecal urgency or incontinence, or gaps/bulging in the incision or midline, stop exercise and contact the OB/physio.
- This plan is conservative and meant for an uncomplicated recovery. If diastasis recti (DR) or pelvic floor dysfunction is suspected, refer to a pelvic health physiotherapist for assessment and tailored rehab.
- Progress only with symptoms-free response: if symptoms (pain, heaviness, pressure, urinary leakage, increased bleeding) occur, regress intensity/frequency and get a professional evaluation.

Overview — 12 weeks divided into three phases:
- Phase A (Weeks 1–2 of program = postpartum weeks 4–5): Healing & reconditioning — light walking, breathing, gentle pelvic floor activation, mobility. No direct abdominal loading.
- Phase B (Weeks 3–6 of program = postpartum weeks 6–9): Early rebuilding after typical 6‑week clearance — introduce gentle core re-education, more strength for posterior chain and glutes, low-load functional strength. Progress only if OB clears at week 6.
- Phase C (Weeks 7–12 of program = postpartum weeks 10–15): Progressive strengthening and reintroduction of higher-load and dynamic activities as tolerated, including more intentional ab and functional training, gradual return toward higher intensity conditioning by week 12 if symptom-free.

General session structure (each session): 5–10 min breathing & gentle warm-up → main body of work (strength/mobility/conditioning) → cool-down and scar mobility if appropriate → pelvic floor gentle reconnection and relaxation. Aim for 3 nonconsecutive sessions per week (e.g., Mon/Wed/Fri) plus daily short walks and mobility. Start with 2–3 short walks daily as tolerated during Phase A.

Progression principles:
- Pain and symptom guided: progress only if no worsening of pelvic pressure, pain, or incontinence.
- Start with low load and higher focus on movement quality, breathing, pelvic floor coordination.
- Use tempo, range, and repetitions before adding external load (since home/no equipment).
- By Phase C, increase difficulty via single‑leg variations, tempo changes, increased reps/sets, and plyo only when cleared and symptom-free.

- Aim for adequate protein to support tissue repair and strength rebuilding: ~1.2–1.6 g/kg bodyweight per day if not breastfeeding; if breastfeeding, aim at upper end (~1.6–2.0 g/kg) and ensure additional calories (approx +300 kcal/day, individualized).

Phase A — Healing & reconditioning (Program weeks 1–2 = postpartum weeks 4–5)

Below is a practical, evidence-based nutrition plan you can give your client to support breastfeeding while she follows the 12‑week postpartum exercise program. It focuses on adequate energy, higher protein, key micronutrients, hydration, and meal/timing strategies for postpartum recovery and milk supply. Encourage she checks this with her medical provider or a registered dietitian if she has allergies, special dietary needs, or complications.

Key energy and macronutrient targets
- Calories: aim for roughly an additional ~300–500 kcal/day above her pre‑pregnancy needs to support milk production. A common practical target is total daily energy ≈ pre‑pregnancy maintenance + ~350 kcal. If she is underweight or producing very high milk volumes, aim toward the higher end (~500 kcal/day extra). If she’s already overweight, use a conservative deficit approach while ensuring supply and symptoms are monitored (avoid aggressive calorie restriction).
- Protein: 1.6–2.0 g/kg body weight per day is a good target while breastfeeding and exercising. Example: if she weighs 70 kg, aim for ~112–140 g protein/day.
- Carbohydrate: moderate to support energy for workouts and lactation — aim for ~40–55% of daily calories from carbs (focus on whole grains, fruit, starchy vegetables).
- Fat: include healthy fats to support calorie needs, essential fatty acids, and satiation (about 25–35% of calories). Aim to include omega‑3 (especially DHA) sources.

Micronutrients to prioritize
- Iron: postpartum iron stores may be low, especially with delivery blood loss. Include iron‑rich foods (lean red meat, poultry, legumes, fortified cereals) and pair with vitamin C to enhance absorption. If she was prescribed iron, continue as directed.
- Calcium: 1000 mg/day (same as pre-pregnancy for most adults). Dairy, fortified plant milks, leafy greens, tofu, and canned fish with bones are good sources.
- Vitamin D: 600–800 IU/day (some breastfeeding mothers may require higher doses if deficient); consider supplementation per clinician labs.
- Iodine: breastfeeding increases iodine needs — aim for ~250 mcg/day. Use iodized salt and iodine-rich foods (dairy, fish, seaweed in moderation) or a multivitamin containing iodine.
- DHA/Omega‑3: 200–300 mg DHA/day recommended for lactating women. Sources: low‑mercury fatty fish (salmon, sardines), algal DHA supplements if vegetarian/vegan.
- B12: if vegetarian/vegan or if low, supplement per clinician advice.

Hydration
- Drink to thirst, but make hydration convenient around feeds/workouts. A general guide: aim for at least 2.0–3.0 L fluid/day; more if sweating heavily or producing a lot of milk.
- Keep a water bottle nearby when feeding; have a glass of water with each feed.
- Include electrolytes (salty snack or sports drink) after very long or sweaty sessions.

Meal structure and sample day
Aim for regular meals and snacks to support energy and steady milk supply. Prioritize nutrient-dense choices and easy-to-prepare options.

Sample daily template (adjust portions for calorie target)
- Breakfast
  - Oats with milk/yogurt, sliced banana, a tablespoon of almond or peanut butter, and a sprinkle of chia seeds (protein + carbs + healthy fat + fiber + omega‑3)
  - Glass of water

- Mid-morning snack
  - Greek yogurt with berries and a handful of mixed nuts OR a whole‑grain toast with avocado and cottage cheese

- Lunch
  - Grilled chicken or chickpea salad with mixed greens, quinoa or brown rice, roasted vegetables, olive oil vinaigrette
  - Piece of fruit
  - Water

- Afternoon snack (good to have before/after a workout or breastfeeding session)
  - Smoothie: milk (or fortified plant milk), 1 scoop protein powder (whey or plant), spinach, frozen fruit, tablespoon nut butter
  - OR hummus + whole grain crackers + carrot sticks

- Dinner
  - Baked salmon (or tofu) + sweet potato + steamed broccoli or a green vegetable + side salad
  - Include a source of starch, protein, and vegetables

- Evening snack (if needed)
  - Cottage cheese with fruit, or peanut butter on apple slices, or a small bowl of fortified cereal with milk

Examples of quick, high-protein postpartum snacks
- Hard‑boiled eggs
- Greek yogurt with honey and oats
- Cottage cheese with fruit
- Protein bars (choose low-sugar, whole‑food options)
- Tuna/sardines on wholegrain crackers
- Smoothies with milk and protein powder
- Trail mix with nuts, seeds, and dried fruit

Supplement suggestions (discuss with clinician)
- Prenatal/postnatal multivitamin that contains iodine and adequate B12 if deficient.
- DHA supplement (200–300 mg/day) if intake from fish is low.
- Vitamin D supplement if deficient or limited sun exposure.
- Continue iron supplement if prescribed postpartum.

Foods & habits to support milk supply (evidence-based cautious approach)
- Most lactation guidance emphasizes that overall caloric and fluid adequacy are important. Traditional galactagogues (oats, fenugreek, blessed thistle) have mixed evidence — they may help some people but aren’t required; use them only if she wants to try and with clinician awareness (fenugreek can interact with medical conditions/meds and can affect baby’s smell/taste).
- Regular feeding/pumping and emptying of the breast is the strongest factor in maintaining supply.
- Avoid sudden aggressive calorie restriction and very low-carb diets soon after birth; those can reduce supply in some women.

Practical tips for combining breastfeeding and exercise
- Time a snack and a feed/pump around workouts: have a light carb + protein snack 30–60 min before or a recovery snack within 30–60 min after.
- If breasts are full and uncomfortable during exercise, a quick pump or feed before the session can increase comfort.
- Wear a supportive nursing sports bra during workouts.
- If baby is sensitive to certain foods (rare), and you notice fussiness or rash after maternal intake of a particular food, consider tracking and adjusting diet with help from a clinician.

Weight loss while breastfeeding
- Aim for gradual weight loss (~0.5–1.0 lb/week) if weight loss is desired; larger deficits can risk lowering milk supply.
- A modest deficit of ~300–500 kcal/day below estimated total energy expenditure (including the ~350 kcal for lactation) is typically safe for gradual weight loss but must be individualized and monitored.
- Prioritize protein and nutrient density over strict calorie cutting.

Monitoring and when to refer
- Ask the client to monitor milk supply changes (wet diapers, weight gain if closely followed by pediatrician), infant behavior, and her own energy and mood.
- If she notices decreased milk supply after dietary changes or exercise increases, reduce intensity/caloric deficit and consult lactation support.
- Refer to a registered dietitian or lactation consultant for personalized plans, allergy concerns, vegan/vegetarian needs, or persistent supply questions.

- Heel slides with shallow TA draw: 2–3 x 8–10 each side. Keep spine neutral; stop if doming.
- Heel taps (supine): knees bent, lower one heel a few cm then return — 2–3 x 8–10 each.
- Bird‑dog (hands & knees): 2–3 x 6–8 each side with 2–3 s hold, focus on neutral spine and breathing.

Progression rules: only increase reps or add 1–2 holds if no bulging, heaviness or leakage.

- Dead‑bug progression: start with arms only (legs stationary) → alternating single-leg lowerings. 3 sets x 6–8 each side. Cue: ribs soft, lower back stays neutral, exhale on lowering, gentle pelvic‑floor lift.

- Increase plank time by 10–15 s increments to max 60 s on knees before progressing to full plank.
- Add dead‑bug range (lower leg lower toward floor) gradually.

Goals: introduce loaded core work and standing anti‑rotation/anti‑extension patterns integrated with functional lifts.

- Farmer carries (heavy backpack) — 3 x 40–90 s. Great for anti‑lateral flexion and functional core loading.
- Pallof press with increased resistance/longer holds — 3 x 10–12 each side.
- Dead‑bug with light held weight in hands for added challenge — 3 x 8 each side.

- Increase load (backpack, heavier water bottles) for carries and standing core work before increasing time under tension for floor-based abdominal exercises.

- Push-ups progression: 4 x 10–12.

- Phase 2 (Weeks 5–7): dead-bug progressions, modified planks, Pallof presses, side plank (knees), monitor for doming.

- New or increased pelvic heaviness/pressure.
- Urinary leakage or urgency with exercises.
- Increased incision pain, redness, or systemic symptoms.

- Fats: include omega‑3s (200–300 mg DHA/day).

- Micronutrients: ensure iron, iodine, vitamin D, calcium and B12 adequacy. Continue prenatal/postnatal multivitamin if recommended.
- Sleep: prioritize rest; naps when possible. Sleep loss impacts recovery and pelvic floor function.
- Avoid aggressive calorie restriction; aim for gradual weight loss only if desired and monitored.

Below is a consolidated, ready-to-use 12‑week postpartum return-to-exercise program for your client (33 F, 4 weeks post uncomplicated C‑section at start). It combines the conservative start (pre‑6‑week), the post‑6‑week cleared progressions, the later no‑jump restriction (cleared for moderate exercise but no jumping for four more weeks), the added early-week strength detail, and the stepwise core reintroduction. Keep using symptom guidance throughout. I’ve written it as week‑by‑week sessions (3 structured sessions/week + walking/cardio) with exercises, sets/reps, progressions, breathing/pelvic‑floor cues, and nutrition/recovery reminders.

Important safety reminders before use
- Continue to watch for pelvic heaviness/pressure, urinary/fecal leakage, midline bulging (coning), increased incision pain, fever, or increased bleeding. If any occur, stop and consult OB/pelvic‑floor physio.
- Progress only if symptom‑free. Regress to earlier, supine, or bilateral work if symptoms appear.
- She is breastfeeding: maintain extra ~300–500 kcal/day and 1.6–2.0 g/kg/day protein (use earlier nutrition plan).
- For breathing/pelvic‑floor cue on every set: inhale to prepare (rib expansion), exhale on exertion with a gentle pelvic‑floor lift and TA draw-in (short, light lift); avoid breath‑holding/strong Valsalva. Relax fully between sets.

Weekly structure (applies all weeks)
- Strength sessions: 3 nonconsecutive days/week (e.g., Mon/Wed/Fri).
- Low-moderate cardio: daily short walks early weeks (15–30 min/day), progress to 2 brisk walks or cycling sessions/week (20–40 min) as tolerated once cleared.
- Mobility & breathing: 5–10 min at start/end of each session.
- Core blocks: integrated each session per week plan below.
- Symptom log: client records pelvic symptoms, incision pain, sleep, and energy each week.

Weeks 1–2 (Program start: postpartum weeks 4–5) — Healing & reconditioning (pre‑6‑week, light activity only)
Goal: gentle walking, breathing/pelvic‑floor reconnect, mobility, light activation. No direct abdominal loading, no heavy lifting, no jumping.

Daily
- Walk in short bouts total 15–30 min/day as tolerated.
- Hydration and protein focus per nutrition plan.

Sessions (3x/week, ~15–25 min each)
Session A — Posterior chain & activation
- Warm-up: Diaphragmatic breathing 4–6 breaths; cat/cow 6–8; shoulder rolls.
- Glute bridge (double-leg): 2–3 x 8–12. Cue: exhale on lift, gentle pelvic‑floor lift.
- Heel slides (supine): 2 x 8–10 each side (soft TA draw-in).
- Standing hip abduction (support): 2 x 10–12 each.
- Scapular retractions: 2 x 10–12.
- Cool-down: pelvic‑floor relaxation 3 lifts and full relax; gentle hamstring stretch.

Session B — Mobility & upper-body
- Warm-up: breathing + thoracic rotation 6–8 each.
- Seated/standing towel rows: 2 x 10–12.
- Incline wall push-ups: 2 x 8–12.
- Side-lying clamshells: 2 x 12 each.
- Calf raises: 2 x 12–15.
- Cool-down: pelvic‑floor relaxation.

Session C — Functional lower body
- Warm-up: breathing + hip circles.
- Sit-to-stand (chair): 2–3 x 8–10 (slow).
- Assisted reverse lunges: 2 x 6–8 each.
- Bridge march (alternating knee lifts in bridge): 2 x 8–10 total.
- Side step-outs: 2 x 10–12 each.
- Cool-down: pelvic‑floor relaxation.

Progressions across Weeks 1–2
- Increase sets from 2 → 3, reps +2 where tolerated and symptom-free.
- Keep exercises supine or supported when possible. No abdominal exercises beyond gentle heel slides and pelvic tilts.

Weeks 3–6 (Program weeks 3–6; postpartum weeks 6–9) — Early rebuilding (start only after 6‑week appointment clearance)
Note: begin only once OB clearance is confirmed (she’s now cleared at week 6). Continue to avoid impact/jumping until advised. Start core reconnection here per core reintroduction plan.

Overall goals: introduce gentle core re‑education, add light loading and unilateral control, increase walking/cardio to 20–40 min most days, build strength foundation.

Weekly frequency: 3x strength sessions/week + 2 short cardio walks.

Detailed weekly plan (progress each week):

Week 3 (first week post‑clearance)
Session 1 — Posterior chain & core re‑education (~25–30 min)
- Warm-up: diaphragmatic breathing 5 reps; cat/cow; thoracic rotations.
- Glute bridge: 3 x 10–12 (progress to 1–2 s hold).
- Heel slides with soft TA: 3 x 8–10 each.
- Bird‑dog (hands & knees): 3 x 6–8 each (2–3 s hold).
- Wall push-ups: 3 x 8–10.
- Core: supine pelvic tilts 2 x 8 and 4–6 breathing coordination reps.
- Cool-down: pelvic‑floor relax.

Session 2 — Standing strength & scapula (~25–30 min)
- Romanian hinge (bodyweight): 3 x 8–10 (practice hip hinge).
- Standing hip abduction: 3 x 10–12 each.
- Bent-over 1-arm row (water bottle): 3 x 10 each.
- Wall sit or supported shallow squat: 3 x 20–30 s.
- Scapular squeezes or prone T’s: 2 x 8–10.
- Cool-down.

Session 3 — Functional & balance (~25–30 min)
- Sit-to-stand slow: 3 x 8–10.
- Reverse lunge assisted: 3 x 8 each.
- Heel taps or heel slides: 3 x 8–10.
- Side-lying clamshells: 3 x 12 each.
- Gentle walk 15–20 min.

Week 4
- Increase unilateral work: progress some bridges to single-leg partials; add bridge march variations (3 x 10–12).
- Add bird-dog holds 3 s and increase rows to 3 x 12.
- Introduce light loaded household items (0.5–2 kg) only for upper-body rows/presses if movement quality uncompromised.
- Core: begin dead‑bug progression (arms only or one leg at a time): 2–3 x 6–8 each.

Week 5
- Progress squatting and hinge variations: assisted split-stance RDLs 3 x 8 each.
- Add step-ups onto low step 3 x 8–10 if balance good.
- Push-ups progress: incline → counter → knee push-ups 3 x 8–10.
- Core: Modified plank on knees 2–3 x 10–20 s (only if no doming); Pallof press light 2 x 8 each side.

Week 6
- Consolidate: increase sets to 3–4 for primary lifts (bridges, rows, RDLs).
- Introduce controlled single-leg RDLs 3 x 8 each (bodyweight or light load).
- Core: dead-bug 3 x 6–8, Pallof press 3 x 8–10, continue modified plank progression.
- Cardio: 2 x 20–30 min brisk walk.

Progression/caution through Weeks 3–6
- Increase reps/sets before adding load. Use household load only when technique clean.
- Stop any exercise that triggers pelvic‑floor symptoms; regress to supine/bilateral low-load work.

Weeks 7–12 (Program weeks 7–12; postpartum weeks 10–15) — Progressive strengthening & conditioning, no jumping for 4 more weeks (as per OB)
Goal: build strength, endurance and low-impact power, progressively increase load and complexity while avoiding jumping/impact for four weeks. Continue core progression as below.

Weekly format: 3 strength sessions/week (40–50 min) + 2 cardio sessions (20–40 min) + 1 mobility/recovery session optional.

Weeks 7–8 (first 2 post-clearance months adjusted)
General: move toward heavier household loading (backpack, milk jugs), more unilateral work, tempo manipulation, and controlled concentric power (explode up but stay grounded).

Week 7
Session Lower — Strength & low‑impact power
- Warm-up: breathing + mobility 8 min.
- Goblet squat (backpack): 4 x 8–10 (3 s down, explode up; no jump).
- Romanian deadlift (backpack or bottles): 3 x 8–10.
- Bulgarian split squat (bodyweight → hold load): 3 x 8 each.
- Hip thrust (elevated): 3 x 10–12.
- Farmer carry (backpack): 3 x 40–60 s.
Core: bird-dog 3 x 8 each; dead-bug 3 x 6–8.

Session Upper — Strength & posture
- Incline → knee push-ups: 4 x 8–12.
- Single-arm bent-over row: 3 x 10 each.
- Single-arm overhead press: 3 x 10 each.
- Scapular T/Y/I: 3 x 8–10.
- Glute bridge march: 3 x 12 total.
Core: Pallof press 3 x 10 each side.

Session Full-body — Tempo & control
- Step-ups (slow down): 3 x 10 each.
- Single-leg RDL: 3 x 8–10 each.
- Elevated/negative-focused push-ups: 3 x 8–10.
- Bent-over rows: 3 x 10–12.
- Glute bridges: 3 x 12.
Core: side-lying plank (knees) 3 x 20–30 s each.

Cardio: 2 x 20–30 min brisk walks; optional easy bike.

Week 8
- Increase sets or load slightly: e.g., goblet squats 4 x 8 (add more weight in backpack), Bulgarian splits 4 x 8, hip thrusts 4 x 10–12.
- Add circuit-style low-impact conditioning session: 3 rounds of reverse lunges, incline push-ups, single-leg deadlifts, rows, Pallof presses (45 s on / 15 s rest) — moderate pace, focus on form.
- Core: begin full plank if no doming: 3 x 10–20 s → build to 3 x 30 s over weeks.

Weeks 9–10 (build strength and low‑impact power)
Focus: heavy-ish sets for strength, longer carries, more unilateral loading, tempo contrast.

Week 9

- Bulgarian split squat weighted: 4 x 8 each.
- Single-leg RDL heavier: 4 x 8–10 each.
- Hip thrust (heavier backpack): 4 x 8–10.
- Push-ups progression: 4 x 10–12.
- Bent-over rows heavier: 4 x 10–12.

Cardio: 2 x 30–35 min brisk walk or bike.

Week 10
- Use tempo contrast: long eccentrics (3–4 s) and fast concentric on squats/lunges without leaving ground. Increase farmer carry times (3 x 60–75 s).
- Add standing anti-rotation progression: Pallof press with squat or march integration.
- Core: dead-bug weighted 3 x 8; side plank 3 x 30 s.

Weeks 11–12 (consolidation; still no jumping until 4-week no-jump window passes)
Goal: consolidate strength gains, prepare for possible reintroduction of impact after no-jump period ends.

Week 11
- Heavy lower day: Goblet squats 4 x 6–8 (heavier), RDL 4 x 6–8, Bulgarian split squat 3 x 8, hip thrust 4 x 8–10.
- Upper day: Push/row supersets 4 rounds; overhead press; scapular work.
- Full-body/conditioning: circuit of single-leg RDLs, step-ups, rows, push-ups, core anti-rotation.
Core: combine farmer carries (3 x 75–90 s) and dynamic Pallof variations.

Week 12
- Consolidation week. Test strength markers (e.g., controlled single-leg RDL x 8 each with heavier backpack; goblet squat 4 x 6–8 heavier). Continue no jumping.
- Cardio: 2 x 30–40 min moderate sessions; 1 mobility/recovery session.

Core reintroduction (integrated across Weeks 3–12)
Follow the stepwise core plan below (already integrated above by week numbers). Use it as the authoritative progression for all core work in sessions.

- Phase 1 (Weeks 3–4 post‑clearance): breathing coordination, pelvic tilts, heel slides, bird-dog, glute bridges.
- Phase 2 (Weeks 5–7): dead-bug progressions, modified planks, Pallof presses, side plank (knees), monitor for doming.
- Phase 3 (Weeks 8–10): full plank if safe, weighted dead-bug, farmer carries, Pallof with longer holds, integration into compound lifts.
- Phase 4 (Weeks 11–12): dynamic trunk work, anti‑extension rollouts (if safe), heavier loaded carries and integrated power without impact.

Signs to regress core work immediately
- Any midline doming/coning during exercise.
- New or increased pelvic heaviness/pressure.
- Urinary leakage or urgency with exercises.
- Increased incision pain, redness, or systemic symptoms.

Nutrition & recovery (summary)
- Energy: +300–500 kcal/day above pre‑pregnancy maintenance to support breastfeeding and training.
- Protein: 1.6–2.0 g/kg/day.
- Carbohydrates: moderate, increase around workouts for energy.
- Fats: include omega‑3s (200–300 mg DHA/day).
- Hydration: at least 2–3 L/day; sip water during feeds and workouts.
- Micronutrients: ensure iron, iodine, vitamin D, calcium and B12 adequacy. Continue prenatal/postnatal multivitamin if recommended.
- Sleep: prioritize rest; naps when possible. Sleep loss impacts recovery and pelvic floor function.
- Avoid aggressive calorie restriction; aim for gradual weight loss only if desired and monitored.

Breathing & pelvic‑floor cues (every session)
- Inhale to prepare (rib expansion), exhale on exertion with a gentle pelvic‑floor lift and TA draw‑in (~1–2 s), then fully relax between repetitions/sets.
- Do 3–5 full relax breaths after heavy sets to reset pelvic floor tone.
- Avoid breath‑holding/straining. If lifting heavier, cue smaller exhalations rather than full Valsalva.

Symptom monitoring & regression rules
- If any new leakage, heaviness, or midline bulging: stop progressions, reduce load/volume, return to more supine/bilateral work, and consult pelvic‑floor physiotherapist if persists >1–2 weeks.
- If incision pain/redness/fever: stop exercise and consult OB.
- Track symptoms 24–48 hours after increasing load; if symptoms appear, reduce intensity and re-evaluate.

When to reintroduce jumping/impact
- She was advised no jumping for 4 more weeks from clearance; reintroduce only after that no‑jump period has ended AND:
  - She is completely symptom‑free (no leakage, heaviness, doming).
  - She has good tolerances to single‑leg power and rapid concentric drills (fast step-ups, rapid calf raises) without symptoms.
  - Ideally cleared by a pelvic‑floor physio for impact if you plan to resume running, plyometrics or heavy maximal lifts.
- Reintroduction plan (after clearance): start with low-volume, low-height drills, progressive landing volume over 3–4 weeks, and continue pelvic-floor monitoring.

Coaching tips & tracking
- Use video or live observation for doming and breath pattern during core and exertional moves.
- Log RPE, pelvic symptoms, incision complaints, sleep, and training load weekly.
- Progress reps → sets → load → tempo → unilateral complexity (in that order) when symptom-free.
